Models, the cache, and custom models

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/models-and-cache.Rmd
models-and-cache.Rmd

A sentence embedding is only as reproducible as the model that computed it. Two analyses that both say they used “all-MiniLM-L6-v2” can disagree if one downloaded the model a year later, after the repository was updated, or if a file was truncated in transit. The choice of model also shapes the result: models differ in the languages they were trained on, in the length of text they read, and in the size of the vectors they return, and each of these limits what an analysis can ask of the embeddings.

sbert treats the model as part of the method. Each supported model is pinned to an immutable revision of its Hugging Face repository and to the size and SHA-256 hash of every file, downloads happen only when asked for, and every file is verified before it is used. This guide covers the registry of pinned models and how to choose among them, installing the runtime and a model, the cache in which models are kept, scripts that run without a person to answer a prompt, and models outside the registry.

library(sbert)
#> sbert 0.6.0: Sentence-BERT embeddings and topic models in R.
#>   14 pinned models (see models()); default: all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
#>   A model is downloaded only on request, once, and verified by SHA-256.

Data

The data of this guide is the registry of pinned models, returned by models(). Reading it needs no download and no network.

  • model: the name passed to load_model(), encode() and the topic verbs.
  • dimensions: the length of each embedding vector.
  • max_tokens: the longest input the model reads, in its sub-word tokens; longer inputs are truncated.
  • languages: the languages the model was trained for.
  • size_mb: the download size in megabytes.
models()
#>                                    model dimensions max_tokens      languages size_mb
#> 1                       all-MiniLM-L6-v2        384        256        English    90.9
#> 2                      all-MiniLM-L12-v2        384        128        English   133.6
#> 3                paraphrase-MiniLM-L3-v2        384        128        English    69.5
#> 4              multi-qa-MiniLM-L6-cos-v1        384        512        English    90.9
#> 5  paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2        384        128  50+ languages   479.4
#> 6                      all-mpnet-base-v2        768        384        English   436.3
#> 7  paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2        768        128  50+ languages  1119.2
#> 8                      bge-small-en-v1.5        384        512        English   133.8
#> 9                       bge-base-en-v1.5        768        512        English   436.5
#> 10                 multilingual-e5-small        384        512 100+ languages   487.4
#> 11                 nomic-embed-text-v1.5        768       8192        English   548.0
#> 12           jina-embeddings-v2-small-en        512       8192        English   130.5
#> 13                  mxbai-embed-large-v1       1024        512        English  1337.6
#> 14                        potion-base-8M        256    1000000        English    30.9

The registry pins 14 models. They return vectors of 256 to 1024 dimensions and take from 30.9 MB to 1,338 MB of disk. The default, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, returns 384 dimensions, reads 256 tokens and takes 90.9 MB.

Which model fits the corpus?

Three properties decide the choice: the languages of the texts, their length, and the cost the analysis can bear. The language comes first: an English model embeds text in other languages poorly, and texts in two languages that mean the same thing are close only in a multilingual model.

subset(models(), languages != "English")
#>                                    model dimensions max_tokens      languages size_mb
#> 5  paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2        384        128  50+ languages     479
#> 7  paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2        768        128  50+ languages    1119
#> 10                 multilingual-e5-small        384        512 100+ languages     487

Of the pinned models, 3 are multilingual. The two paraphrase-multilingual models read 128 tokens, about a long sentence; multilingual-e5-small reads 512. For an English corpus, length is the next question.

subset(models(), max_tokens >= 512)
#>                          model dimensions max_tokens      languages size_mb
#> 4    multi-qa-MiniLM-L6-cos-v1        384        512        English    90.9
#> 8            bge-small-en-v1.5        384        512        English   133.8
#> 9             bge-base-en-v1.5        768        512        English   436.5
#> 10       multilingual-e5-small        384        512 100+ languages   487.4
#> 11       nomic-embed-text-v1.5        768       8192        English   548.0
#> 12 jina-embeddings-v2-small-en        512       8192        English   130.5
#> 13        mxbai-embed-large-v1       1024        512        English  1337.6
#> 14              potion-base-8M        256    1000000        English    30.9

Of the pinned models, 8 read 512 tokens or more, and nomic-embed-text-v1.5 and jina-embeddings-v2-small-en read 8,192, more than a research abstract needs. potion-base-8M lists 1,000,000 because it has no window at all: it is a static model that looks up a vector for each token and averages them, without a neural network. It is the smallest model in the registry, needs no ONNX Runtime, and replaces the transformer with a table lookup, but averaging ignores word order, so “the teacher helped the student” and “the student helped the teacher” get the same vector. A long-window model is one answer to long documents; splitting them into sentences, covered in the guide to segmenting long documents, is the other, and it works with every model.

models(detail = TRUE) adds the technical settings that encode() applies automatically.

subset(models(detail = TRUE),
       select = c(model, pooling, prefix, engine, license))
#>                                    model pooling            prefix engine    license
#> 1                       all-MiniLM-L6-v2    mean                     onnx Apache-2.0
#> 2                      all-MiniLM-L12-v2    mean                     onnx Apache-2.0
#> 3                paraphrase-MiniLM-L3-v2    mean                     onnx Apache-2.0
#> 4              multi-qa-MiniLM-L6-cos-v1    mean                     onnx Apache-2.0
#> 5  paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2    mean                     onnx Apache-2.0
#> 6                      all-mpnet-base-v2    mean                     onnx Apache-2.0
#> 7  paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2    mean                     onnx Apache-2.0
#> 8                      bge-small-en-v1.5     cls                     onnx        MIT
#> 9                       bge-base-en-v1.5     cls                     onnx        MIT
#> 10                 multilingual-e5-small    mean           query:    onnx        MIT
#> 11                 nomic-embed-text-v1.5    mean search_document:    onnx Apache-2.0
#> 12           jina-embeddings-v2-small-en    mean                     onnx Apache-2.0
#> 13                  mxbai-embed-large-v1     cls                     onnx Apache-2.0
#> 14                        potion-base-8M    mean                   static        MIT

pooling is how token vectors become one text vector: the mean of all tokens, or the vector of the first (cls) token, as each model was trained. prefix is text that two models expect before every input ("query: " for multilingual-e5-small, "search_document: " for nomic-embed-text-v1.5); encode() adds it, so the caller passes the text alone. engine separates the transformer models (onnx) from the static one. The licenses are Apache-2.0 or MIT. The full Hugging Face id and the pinned revision are in the columns id and revision.

Dimension has a cost: memory and k-means time grow with it. A corpus of 100,000 texts at 1,024 dimensions takes 819.2 MB as a matrix of doubles (8 bytes per value), against 307.2 MB at 384. A larger model is worth its cost when a comparison on the corpus, for example with compare_topics(), shows it separates the themes better (see choosing the number of topics).

What does a first run need?

A transformer model needs the native ONNX Runtime, which the onnxr package installs on request. The model’s files are then downloaded once. Neither step happens during installation or loading of sbert, and neither is run in this guide.

install_runtime()                         # once per machine
model_download("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")        # once per model
model <- load_model("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
embeddings <- encode(c("A first sentence.", "A second one."), model)

install_runtime() passes cuda to onnxr::onnx_install(): FALSE asks for the portable CPU runtime, TRUE for CUDA where it is supported, and NULL (the default) detects which. model_download() fetches only the files that are missing or fail verification, writes each to a temporary file, checks its size and SHA-256 hash, and moves it into the cache only if both match. load_model() never downloads: it loads files already in the cache, verifies them again (verify = TRUE), and stops with an error of class sbert_model_not_installed when a file is missing, sbert_cache_invalid when one fails verification, and sbert_runtime_missing when a transformer model is loaded without ONNX Runtime. The static potion-base-8M is loaded without the runtime.

Verbs that take a model name, such as encode(text, model = "bge-small-en-v1.5"), load it themselves and keep it for the rest of the session. If it is not installed, an interactive session asks once whether to download it, giving the size and license.

Where are the models kept?

All models live in one cache per user, outside any project, at the location R designates for the package’s cached files.

cache_dir()
#> [1] "/home/runner/.cache/R/sbert"

cache_dir() returns the path from tools::R_user_dir("sbert", which = "cache") and creates nothing. Inside it, each pinned model has a directory named after the model and its revision, so two revisions can never be mixed. model_status() lists the files a model needs and checks them.

subset(model_status(model = "all-MiniLM-L6-v2"),
       select = c(file, exists, valid, expected_bytes, actual_bytes))
#>             file exists valid expected_bytes actual_bytes
#> 1     model.onnx   TRUE  TRUE       90405214     90405214
#> 2 tokenizer.json   TRUE  TRUE         466247       466247
subset(model_status(model = "potion-base-8M"),
       select = c(file, exists, valid, expected_bytes, actual_bytes))
#>                file exists valid expected_bytes actual_bytes
#> 1 model.safetensors  FALSE FALSE       30236760           NA
#> 2    tokenizer.json  FALSE FALSE         683666           NA
#> 3       config.json  FALSE FALSE            202           NA

The default model consists of model.onnx and tokenizer.json; the static model of an embedding table (model.safetensors), a tokenizer and a configuration file. On the machine that built this page no model is installed, so every file is reported missing (exists is TRUE) and invalid. valid is true only when the file has the pinned size and hash; model_status() only reads, so calling it is safe at any time. The path column, left out here, gives where each file is expected.

cache_size()
#> [1] 90871461

cache_size() is the number of bytes used by all files under the cache, here 9.087^{7} because nothing has been downloaded. Models are kept until they are removed, and model_remove() deletes the directory of one pinned model; other models and custom models are untouched.

model_remove(model = "all-mpnet-base-v2")

Every one of these functions takes cache_dir, so a project can keep its models elsewhere, for example on a shared drive, by passing the same path to model_download(), model_status() and load_model().

Scripts that run unattended

A script run with Rscript, a scheduled job or a knitted report has no one to answer the download prompt. In such a session a missing model is an error of class sbert_model_not_installed, never a silent download. There are two ways to allow the download.

# Either install explicitly, once, before the analysis runs ...
model_download("all-MiniLM-L6-v2", quiet = TRUE)

# ... or allow this script to download any model it needs.
options(sbert.download = TRUE)
embeddings <- encode(c("A first sentence.", "A second one."))

With options(sbert.download = TRUE), a verb that needs a missing model calls model_download() itself, with the same verification as an explicit download. The explicit call is the better choice for a shared or published analysis: the script then states which models it depends on.

Models outside the registry

load_custom() loads any public Hugging Face repository that ships an ONNX export of an encoder and a tokenizer.json. The result is an sbert_model like those from load_model(), so encode(), topics() and every other verb accept it.

gte <- load_custom("thenlper/gte-small")
embeddings <- encode(c("A first sentence.", "A second one."), gte)

# Pin a revision, and state settings that cannot be detected
gte <- load_custom("thenlper/gte-small",
                   revision = "<commit hash>",
                   pooling = "mean", max_length = 512)

A custom model is trusted on first use. On the first call, load_custom() resolves the repository’s current revision (unless revision is given), detects the pooling from the repository’s Sentence-Transformers configuration and the maximum length from sentence_bert_config.json (512 when that file is absent), downloads the two files, and records their sizes and SHA-256 hashes in a local manifest. It stops with an error when the pooling cannot be detected and is not given. A later call with the same revision reads the manifest, verifies the files against it, and does not use the network. A later call without revision first asks Hugging Face for the repository’s current revision; if the repository has changed, that revision is downloaded and recorded as a new model, so an analysis that must not change pins revision. The files are kept under custom/ in the cache directory, one directory per repository and revision, and model_remove() does not delete them. It needs the jsonlite package.

The difference from a pinned model is who vouches for it. The registry’s hashes and settings were fixed by the package; a custom model’s were recorded from whatever the repository held on first download, and the package makes no claim that its embeddings match the original implementation. Passing revision makes the analysis reproducible; checking a few embeddings against the reference implementation, as the verification guide describes for the default model, makes it trustworthy.

Which call for which task

  • See the available models and their settings: models(), models(detail = TRUE).
  • Set up a machine: install_runtime() once, then model_download() for each model the analysis uses.
  • Check an installation without loading it: model_status(); disk use: cache_size(); free space: model_remove().
  • Run a script unattended: model_download() beforehand, or options(sbert.download = TRUE).
  • Use a model not in the registry: load_custom(), with a pinned revision.
  • Encode faster: load_model(threads = "auto") or the static potion-base-8M (see parallel and high-throughput topic modeling).
